1.title: Pull Requests
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: Pull Requests. It covers the exam area Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Follow the Git Hub flow. Open a pull request with a title, description, reviewers and draft state. Review with Comment, Approve and Request changes. Update a P R by merging or ree basing main in. Choose a merge method and know its effect on history. Link issues with closing keywords. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.text: Here is where this module sits in the course. Part: Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Verified with: Git two point five zero.one for the local parts; the Git Hub documentation (read twenty twenty-six-eleven to sixteen) for the Git Hub parts.

1.title: The GitHub flow and opening a pull request
1.text: The Git Hub flow and opening a pull request. A pull request (P R) is Git Hub's place to propose, discuss, review and merge a change. The figure shows the loop.

1.title: The GitHub flow and opening a pull request, continued
1.text: The Git Hub flow and opening a pull request. The figure shows this: The Git Hub flow: create a branch, commit and push, open a pull request, review, merge, then delete the branch.

1.title: The GitHub flow and opening a pull request, continued
1.text: The Git Hub flow and opening a pull request. The official Git Hub flow has six steps. Create a branch with a short, descriptive name. Make changes, commit and push. Create a pull request. A draft is allowed. Address the review comments. Merge. Delete your branch. The P R adds the conversation, in tabs: Conversation, Commits, Checks, Files changed and Findings (automated results). The merge box lists what still blocks the merge, such as missing approvals.

1.title: The GitHub flow and opening a pull request, continued
1.text: The Git Hub flow and opening a pull request. Title. One line that says what changes, like a commit subject. Description. What and why, how you tested it, and closing keywords for issues. Reviewers. People who know the code; only users with write access can request reviews. Draft. For work in progress: it cannot be merged, and code owners are requested only at "Ready for review". Git Hub has two models. In fork and pull, contributors fork the repository and open P Rs against the upstream. In a shared repository, collaborators push topic branches to the same repository. Open a draft P R early: the team sees the direction, and nobody reviews unfinished work.

1.title: Reviews and keeping the branch current
1.text: Reviews and keeping the branch current. A reviewer ends a review with one of three decisions. Comment. Feedback without a verdict. Approve. The change is good to merge. Request changes. The reviewer blocks the merge until the problems are fixed.

1.title: Reviews and keeping the branch current, continued
1.text: Reviews and keeping the branch current. Anyone with read access can review and comment. Admins can require approvals, and code owners are requested automatically. Requesting a team can notify every member; auto assignment or "Only notify requested team members" reduces the noise. Anyone with write access can dismiss a blocking review if its author is away. To answer a review, commit on the same branch and push: the P R follows the branch. When main moves on, bring it into your branch in one of two ways.

1.title: Reviews and keeping the branch current, continued
1.text: Reviews and keeping the branch current. Merge main in. Commands: git fetch, then git merge origin slash main. The next push: A plain git push works. Rebase onto main. Commands: git fetch, then git ree base origin slash main. The next push: Rejected as non-fast-forward, so use git push the force with lease flag. If both sides changed the same lines, Git stops with a conflict. Resolve it locally as in module four: edit the file, remove the markers, git add, then git commit (merge) or git ree base the continue flag (ree base). Push afterwards. Try it. Rebase a P R branch onto the new main, then push it. Your hashes will differ.

1.title: The three merge methods and what they do to history
1.text: The three merge methods and what they do to history. The repository decides which methods are allowed, and merging needs write permission. Here the same three-commit branch is merged three ways into three copies of main. Merge commit. What lands on main: All P R commits plus one merge commit. Your hashes: Kept. Local equivalent: git merge the no ff flag. Squash and merge. What lands on main: One new commit with the whole change. Your hashes: Gone. Local equivalent: git merge the squash flag, then git commit. Rebase and merge. What lands on main: The commits one by one, no merge commit. Your hashes: New S H A s. Local equivalent: git ree base, then a fast-forward.

1.title: The three merge methods and what they do to history, continued
1.text: The three merge methods and what they do to history. The merge commit keeps the whole story, and git log the first parent flag then reads like a list of P Rs. Squash suits short-lived branches, but reusing a squashed branch can cause repeated conflicts. Rebase and merge gives a straight line, but Git Hub's ree base always updates committer information, creates new S H A s and drops empty commits. Try it. The ree based commits keep their subjects but not their hashes.

1.title: The three merge methods and what they do to history, continued
1.text: The three merge methods and what they do to history. All three ways end with identical files. Only the history differs. Tip: After a squash or ree base merge, git branch dash d says "not fully merged". Your branch commits are not in main under their old hashes. Check that the change arrived, then delete with git branch dash D.

1.title: Linking issues, templates and cleaning up
1.text: Linking issues, templates and cleaning up. Closing keywords link a P R to an issue: close, closes, closed, fix, fixes, fixed, resolve, resolves, resolved. Put one in the P R description or a commit message, for instance Closes hash ten or Fixes octo org slash octo repo hash one hundred. They are case-insensitive and the colon is optional. They only work when the P R targets the default branch, and merging into it closes the issue. You can also link up to ten issues by hand in the Development sidebar.

2.title: Linking issues, templates and cleaning up, continued
2.text: Linking issues, templates and cleaning up. A P R template is a file named pull request template dot md in the root, docs slash or dot github slash. Several templates can live in a pull request template slash folder. A template becomes available once it is merged into the default branch. Clean up after the merge. Git Hub shows a "Delete branch" button, and "Restore branch" brings the branch back. Admins can switch on "Automatically delete head branches" in Settings, General, Pull Requests. Then remove the leftovers on your machine. Try it. Delete the remote branch, then prune a branch that was deleted on Git Hub.

2.title: Linking issues, templates and cleaning up, continued
2.text: Linking issues, templates and cleaning up. The warning means the branch matches its remote copy but main lacks its commits: a sign of a squash merge. A fork is a separate repository with its own branches, issues and P Rs; the original is the upstream. Keep it current with git remote add upstream, git fetch upstream and a merge or ree base. The P R branch lives in your fork. The Git Hub C L I does P R steps from a terminal (not run here).

2.title: Linking issues, templates and cleaning up, continued
2.text: Linking issues, templates and cleaning up. Open a pull request. gh pr create. Merge with a chosen method. gh pr merge the squash flag. Add a P R to the merge queue. gh pr merge. Tip: Write Closes hash ten in the P R description, and aim the P R at the default branch. A P R into a release branch will not close the issue.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A three-commit P R is merged with Squash and merge. What does main gain? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: One new commit holding the whole change. Squash and merge turns all P R commits into one commit on the base branch.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. After a squash merge, git branch dash d add cart says the branch is "not fully merged". What is the safest next step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Check that the change is on main, then run git branch dash D add cart. The squash commit is new, so Git cannot see the old commits in main; once you confirm the content arrived, dash D is safe.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A P R says "Fixes hash thirty-one" but targets release slash two dot zero, which is not the default branch. After the merge, issue thirty-one is still open. Why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Closing keywords only work when the P R targets the default branch. Closing keywords act only on P Rs that target the default branch.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Ada ree based her P R branch onto main, and now git push is rejected as non-fast-forward. Which command updates the branch safely? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: git push the force with lease flag, which stops if someone else pushed. The lease check refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Ada opens a draft P R that changes files with a code owner. When will the code owners be requested? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: When she marks the P R as "Ready for review" for them. Code owners are not requested on a draft; marking it ready requests them.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A three-commit P R is merged. git rev list the count flag main grew by three, the merges flag shows zero, and all three hashes changed. Which method was used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Rebase and merge, which replays the commits on top of main. Three new commits with new S H A s and no merge commit is the shape of a ree base merge.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What are the six steps of the Git Hub flow? Answer: Create a branch, commit and push, open a pull request, address review comments, merge, delete the branch. Question two. What are the three review decisions? Answer: Comment, Approve and Request changes. Question three. Which command updates a ree based P R branch safely? Answer: git push the force with lease flag.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which condition must hold for a closing keyword to close an issue? Answer: The P R must target the default branch. Question five. Where can the P R template file live? Answer: In the root, docs slash or dot github slash, named pull request template dot md. Question six. Which two commands delete a branch locally and on the remote? Answer: git branch dash d and git push origin the delete flag.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Git Hub flow: branch, commit and push, P R, review, merge, delete the branch. Opening a P R: title, description, reviewers, draft; a draft cannot merge. Reviews: Comment, Approve, Request changes. Updating: push commits; merge main in, or ree base and the force with lease flag. Merge methods: merge commit keeps all; squash makes one commit; ree base makes new S H A s. Closing keywords: close, fix, resolve; default branch only. Templates: pull request template dot md, in root, docs slash or dot github slash. Cleanup: git branch dash d, git push origin the delete flag, git fetch the prune flag. Forks: P R branch in the fork; upstream remote. If this course is helping you, please subscribe to the channel and hit the bell icon, so you get a notification when the next video is out.
